# Draft:Visual Culture of the Nation of Islam (May, Maia, Sorah, Leyla)

The visual culture of The Nation of Islam (NOI) encompasses newspaper cartoons, fashion and significant public figures, aesthetics, mythological imagery, blending religious symbolism with political messaging. Rooted in Islamic religious practices and a distinctly American context, NOI publications and sequential visual interpretations utilized various mediums, from print media like Muhammad Speaks to fashion and visual mythologies in order to further the Nation’s goals. Visual representations not only conveyed religious teachings but also symbolized resistance to systemic racism and white supremacy, often using stark binary oppositions between Islam and Christianity, and Black empowerment and white oppression. The ideological goals of the Nation of Islam were both manifested through and constructed by these aesthetic forms culminating in a distinctive and powerful visual language.
Muhammad Speaks Newspaper
Muhammad Speaks was likely the Nation of Islam’s largest platform for disseminating imagery and visual materials. Originally called Mr. Muhammad Speaks, it was the Black Muslim newspaper published by the Nation of Islam from 1960 to 1975. Founded under the leadership of Malcolm X, the publication was at one point the largest Black newspaper in the US, covering both secular issues and the teachings of Elijah Muhammad. Almost every issue of the 700 released by the publication included political cartoons that related to both the teachings of Elijah Muhammad and Islam as well as social justice issues, both foreign and domestic. Many of these cartoons were drawn by Eugene Majied, one of the most prominent illustrators of the publication, who worked closely with Elijah Muhammad.
Visual Techniques
The newspaper frequently included images of Elijah Muhammad, both as cartoons and photographs, that depicted him as the leader of not just the Nation of Islam but of Black brotherhood and salvation. According to Christiane Gruber, Muhammad speaks frequently used tactics of “Binary opposition” to “bifurcate hero versus villain, deliverance versus damnation,” positioning the NOI as a savior in contrast to Christianity or other groups who opposed self determination for Black Americans. These binary oppositions were created by literally placing positive images of the NOI directly next to negative images of their opponents. The technique of opposition worked dually to recall historical declaration of Islam and to encourage joining the religion through the removal of a third option. The emphasis on Islam was very important, as the use of visual allegories to Islam worked to both critique the racism of the United States and to extend Islam art to also include the region.
The NOI Flag
The first issue of the newspaper featured an image of the flag of the Nation of Islam, inspired by the Turkish flag, and with the words “justice,” “freedom,” “equality,” and “Islam,” in its four corners. Through the inclusion of Islam in this organization, next to fundamental human aspirations, this imagery cements a visualization of the religion as a core human goal.
Visual Re-Interpretations of Christianity
Visual Aesthetics of the Nation of Islam, particularly in Muhammad Speaks, relied on binary opposition in their visual language. NOI graphic artists visually articulated utopian futures and religious dichotomies in which radiant mosques were able to illuminate the future while the body of a crucified Jesus conveys death and destruction. *Muhammad Speaks* deployed what Christiane Gruber describes as a three-fold iconographic strategy. This was in order to depict Islam as a unifying creed for self-empowerment. Secondly, to promote Islam as superior to Christianity, and “third, to argue that Islam offers the only means for the Black Man, as imagined in the NOI’s conception, to ultimately unshackle himself from the chains of white supremacy and Christian enslavement.”
“Whom Shall You Serve” is a diptych featured in *Muhammad Speaks* vol. 3, no. 26, 11 September 1964, that portrays a distinct visual comparison between Islam and Christianity. On the left, a church is depicted with “Satan?” printed in bold letters. Above, the entry to the church reads “white man’s slavery.” On the right diptych, the question on the last panel is answered by “... or God?” The change in fashion from left to right acts as a stand-in for deliverance from white supremacy and in opposition to Christian oppression. Gruber further notes that the ‘Whom Shall You Serve?’ diptych is one of at least six recurring two-panel comparisons in *Muhammad Speaks* between 1962 and 1964, systematically reinforcing visual dichotomies of deliverance through Islam versus oppression under Christianity.
“Whom Shall You Serve,” also visualizes fashion (further explored in later section) as a form of subverting the hegemonic Christian culture in the United States
Representations of Gender Through Religious Fashion
Fashion played a significant role in the NOI , serving as both a marker of religious identity and a form of resistance to dominant cultural norms. The NOI emphasized modesty, dignity, and discipline through dress, with particular attention placed on the bodies and appearances of its members. For women, this often translated into carefully styled, modest clothing that reflected inner purity and moral conduct. Women wore garments ranging from headscarves that fully concealed their hair to fashionable wraps that allowed for the display of carefully styled bangs, as in the case of Sister Betty, who “refused to look anything but beautiful.”While public modesty was encouraged, head coverings were not universally worn at work, and photographs—from Sister Belinda Boyd at the bakery to university staff—depict a range of practices, from uncovered heads to elaborately tied scarves. The aesthetic choices of women like First Lady Clara Muhammad, whose petite figure was concealed in voluminous garments, suggest both a desire for modesty and a complex visual narrative of visibility and concealment.
The beauty standards for women in the NOI were strict, health and hygiene integral to this aesthetic, with the NOI condemning obesity as a disfiguring legacy of colonialism. Fatness, described as "wrapping undesirable racial bodies," was seen as a visible indicator of moral and spiritual failing, in contrast to the "perfect forms" idealized by NOI Reformers. The emphasis on bodily discipline extended to children, who could be sent home from NOI schools like the University of Islam #4 in Washington D.C. for wearing wrinkled clothes or having unclean fingernails. Uniforms were strictly enforced—girls wore green pantaloons, matching tunics, and white headscarves, monitored by sister captains for cleanliness and presentation.
Fashion was not only a form of religious expression but also a creative outlet. Many Nation girls were introduced to sewing and design early, learning advanced dressmaking techniques in NOI schools, which encouraged the development of a unique Muslim fashion sensibility. These expressions of style and cleanliness were underscored by the principle that "Allah is beautiful, and He loves beauty," extending grooming and sartorial expectations to men as well.Wheeler, Kayla Renée. 2020. “Bowties, Beards, and Boubous: Black Muslim Men's Fashion in the United States —The Revealer.” The Revealer. .  Male members were known for their sharp suits, often accompanied by Elijah Muhammad’s signature bow tie, projecting an image of respectable masculinity that rejected racist stereotypes of Black criminality and poverty. These suits, along with lapel pins bearing Islamic symbols, became both spiritual and social statements, visibly marking the transformation from “the living dead” to faithful Muslims.
Alongside suits, beards and traditional garments like the boubou—long robes of West African origin—became part of a broader visual language of Black Muslim identity. For men, clean grooming, tailored clothing, and deliberate style choices served as a form of "Muslim cool," reflecting religio-racial pride and asserting a dignified presence in public life. These aesthetic forms not only differentiated NOI members from mainstream society but also cultivated an internal culture of beauty, health, and discipline as markers of spiritual and political commitment.
Elijah Muhammad’s Visual Mythology
Elijah Muhammad was responsible for creating “sacred narratives” in the Nation of Islam. This mythology was “countercultural” and relied on post-WWII influences. The visual language included The Mother Plane, later to become Mothership, which would rain fire on Earth at the end of the world, destroying White Civilization, and making it possible for Black people to reign once more.
One of the mythological figures featured in these narratives is Yakub. He is characterized as an evil, mad, and big-headed scientist who launched a series of horrifying genetic experiments resulting in the creation of the white man. Yakub’s story connects to current events of the twentieth century in that it reflected the truth that the medical establishment and the U.S. government had abused and stood silent as Black people were victimized by the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, the state-run program of forced sterilization of poor mothers, and complicity with vigilante and police torture and murder of Black people. The myth of Yakub adopted the terms by which Black people had been rendered inhuman by oppressors and offered a mirror in which they brought life to a reverse ontology, or escape to an alternate reality. A visual depiction of Yakub is featured in The Holy Tablets.
While Elijah Muhammad’s mythology was not an entirely visual form, his thoughts have sparked physical interpretations in pop culture. The mythology of the Mothership has continued outside of the NOI in the form of funk musician George Clinton’s P-Funk Mothership.
Aesthetics of Black Embodiment
The Nation of Islam created particular aesthetics of Black bodies and embodiment in order to reform or dis-identify Black bodies from the “white normative gaze,” created for white pleasure in America. These aesthetics were expressed and produced through the Nation’s politics and cosmographies in order to subvert the ways that Black people have been exploited by whiteness, particularly white Christianity. Not all of these aesthetics were produced through the creation of visual imagery, as ritual and doctrinal claims also worked towards producing claims about the positionality of Black bodies, particularly in relation to the idea of being “out-of-place,” or being “in-place.”
In-place bodies had fixed, racialized identities, either operating at limited capacities within white spheres or adhering to constructions of racial inferiority. The NOI deplored these in-place bodies, as they did not challenge racist systems, and instead sought to create out of place bodies that worked against subverted racist norms. The relationship of positionality in the NOI was not necessarily created through visual imagery, but instead through rhetorical strategies used by members of the Nation for religious and secular purposes. For example, Elijah Muhammad’s claims that the best form of beauty was “spiritual beauty,” accessible through spiritual practices suggest a symbolic and physical aesthetic of beauty to be gained by those that practiced his mode of spirituality, which prioritized Black bodies that subverted white supremacist norms.
The NOI cosmography, likewise, helped to create an aesthetic depiction of Black bodies as transcendent. The mythology of Yakub, in particular, allowed members of the Nation of Islam an outlet through which to reimagine their Blackness. Through a critique of whiteness as created by Yakub, the NOI, and Elijah Muhammad more specifically, critiqued white modes of embodying Black bodies. The story of Yakub reverses traditional white supremacist narratives of God by arguing Black people are the original chosen people of God, reappropriating similar narratives and violences perpetuated by white supremacists in order to assert the aesthetic transcendence of Black bodies. The NOI’s cosmography also worked to remove Black bodies from white power structures by appealing to ideas of life beyond earth: Elijah Muhammad claimed that God told him there were Black people on Mars. By indicating a position of Blackness literally beyond the physical barriers imposed by the world, controlled by white people, Elijah Muhammad suggested a positionality and aesthetic for Blackness beyond that created by white people.
Although the NOI intended to utilize its ideas and aesthetics of Black embodiment in order to subvert white supremacy and empower its members, its re-appropriation of white constructions of race and bodies unintentionally reproduced oppressive narratives and practices, internalizing ideas about class and gender marginalization. The NOI reproduced classist systems originally created by white supremacy, targeting classism at “poor black people and African American Christians,” perpetuated through systems within the Nation that indicated who and whose bodies could be in position of power. In relation to gender, the Nation’s cosmography inextricably links womanhood to wombs, arguing for a particular aesthetic and embodiment of Black womanhood that centers the identities of Black women around motherhood.
Economic Emancipation and 'Do For Self'
One of the foundational tenets in the ideological groundwork of the Nation of Islam was an emphasis on economic separatism: a concept that the Nation’s leaders sought to develop through the establishment of Black-owned businesses and industries like restaurants, farms, shops, and schools.This included the Nation’s ‘Your Supermarket’ brand, which sought to source grocery items directly from NOI farms. The visual branding and advertisement of goods and services sold at ‘Your Supermarket’  locations functioned as a means of cultivating and sustaining Black pride and a desire to uplift Black-owned businesses by patrons, further cementing the importance of economic autonomy within the Nation. Black economic self-sufficiency served as a “key to independence from the white man”, a common rhetoric promoted by the NOI in publications like Muhammad Speaks to encourage Black Americans to envision a separate national identity outside of the oppressive institutions created by and for white people.
This phenomenon was exemplified by the Nation’s ‘Do for Self’ slogan, which sought to promote the socioeconomic advancement of NOI members through adherence to “self-discipline, economic self-sufficiency, and maintaining one’s health through proper diet…”. Visual portrayals of ‘Do for Self’ by political cartoonist Eugene Majied in Muhammad Speaks utilized the slogan as a vehicle for achieving an emancipated future for Black Americans. The employment of the ‘Do for Self’ motif in NOI publications functioned as a tool for which Black communities could visualize steps toward liberation. A political cartoon by Majied titled, ‘The Muslim Way to Success’ represents the ‘Do for Self’ process as an ascension, depicting an individual climbing a ladder (with each rung labelled ‘Do for Self,’ respectively) towards a brighter, more empowered future. Visualizations of a Black utopia guided by a strictly Islamic path (as exemplified by Majied’s illustrations in Muhammad Speaks) served as a mode through which Black readers and NOI members could reevaluate their positionality within the racist sociopolitical structures of the United States.
'Let's Build Our Own House'
The visual motif and slogan, ‘Let’s Build our Own House’  (which appeared in Muhammad Speaks in September of 1964)  similarly communicates the desires of the Nation to uphold a wholly separate economic entity from oppressive pre-established systems. ‘Let’s Build our Own House’ in particular references Elijah Muhammad’s ‘Three Year Economic Program’- an institution created by the Nation that sought to uplift Black and NOI ownership of food distribution chains and supermarkets nationwide. This included, but was not limited to, corporations like ‘Shabazz Foods’ and ‘Shabazz Textile Mills’, which are pictured in the ‘Let’s Build our Own House’  illustration in Muhammad Speaks. The inclusion of NOI-owned supply chains and businesses in the visual elements of the Nation’s publications further spotlights the importance of creating a separatist economic model in order to achieve an independent future.
Media Depictions
During the mid-20th century, the NOI was frequently portrayed by national print media and government agencies as a militant, extremist, and subversive organization, often with alleged communist affiliations. This portrayal was fueled, in part, by semi-factual information routinely leaked to the media by law enforcement agencies such as the FBI during the early 1960s.
Several recurring themes in both governmental and media portrayals of the NOI include depictions of the group as being influenced by foreign entities, as primarily recruiting from prisons and impoverished African American communities, and as being more political than religious in nature. Such narratives framed NOI members as uncritical followers of charismatic, authoritarian leaders, and emphasized the group's radical political stance over its religious identity—despite a lack of concrete evidence to support many of these claims.
In contrast, African American newspapers began offering the NOI a platform to present its own narrative by the mid-1950s. Initially echoing the skepticism of mainstream media, these publications—such as the Pittsburgh Courier, Los Angeles Herald, and New York Amsterdam News—eventually began featuring editorial columns by prominent NOI figures like Elijah Muhammad and Malcolm X. These columns helped reshape public perceptions within Black communities by offering firsthand accounts of the group's beliefs and goals.
Recognizing the power of the press, the NOI also took active steps to counter negative portrayals. As early as 1957, the organization established a public relations fund and department, which led to the founding of Muhammad Speaks, a newspaper dedicated to promoting the group’s image and ideology while countering negative portrayals.
Significant Public Figures
The Nation of Islam’s influence extended into the realm of popular culture, particularly through its association with high-profile figures like Muhammad Ali and Malcolm X.
Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Clay, had been studying the teachings of the NOI since his teenage years in Louisville, Kentucky, and officially joined the movement in the early 1960s. His affiliation became more public following appearances by Malcolm X at his training camp in Miami, prompting widespread media speculation. Muhammad Speaks played a pivotal role in introducing Ali to the Nation of Islam, a move that not only impacted the world of sports but also broader American culture, as Ali became a prominent voice for Black empowerment and a vocal critic of U.S. involvement in Vietnam. By aligning himself with the NOI, Ali challenged prevailing narratives of American exceptionalism, using his celebrity platform to amplify political and religious dissent.
Malcolm X, one of the most media-savvy leaders of the period, strategically engaged with visual and print media to shape public perception of both himself and the NOI. By the time of his assassination in 1965, Malcolm X was among the most photographed and televised African American leaders. His bold, sometimes incendiary rhetoric made him a magnet for mainstream media coverage, which often portrayed him in a sensationalist light.Berger, Maurice. “Malcolm X as Visual Strategist.” The New York Times, September 19, 2012. .  Nevertheless, he utilized Muhammad Speaks and segments of the Black press to convey more nuanced and affirmative representations of the NOI.
A skilled visual strategist, Malcolm X often carried a camera to document the daily life of NOI communities, offering visual counter-narratives to negative media portrayals. He guided photojournalists toward images of family, education, and Black-owned businesses, aiming to contrast with the aggressive headlines he anticipated. He also meticulously curated his public image—from his attire to his rhetoric—understanding that self-presentation was a critical tool in resisting mainstream mischaracterization.
